title: Pictures and Voices

post.author: u/lightbox_linnet
post.title: I catalogue our town's glass plates at night. The catalogue says a woman is watching from the upper window of plate 1142. The window is empty. She is in five more.

blocks.text: I'm the night volunteer at the Wrenmouth Town Photo Archive: two rooms above the old ferry office, a light box, a copy camera, and 9,600 glass-plate negatives from 1880 to 1930. I scan each plate, crop it to the edges of the glass, and get a picture 6384 by 4788 pixels. Then a script sends it to a model, which writes the catalogue description: who is in it, and what the signs say. The Friends of the Archive pay for the model out of the tea-room jar, so the script first shrinks every scan to a thumbnail, 532 by 399 pixels. Mr Treloar, who chairs the Friends, says that keeps it to seventeen cents a night.

Last week the first batch went online: plates 0801 to 1280, 480 plates in four nights of 120. On Saturday a reader wrote to Mr Treloar about plate 1142, this building in 1908, when it was still the ferry office. She wanted to know who the woman was.

PLATE 1142   Ferry office, Quay Street, 1908. Two men at the door; a board reads
             FERRY OFFICE; a woman watching from the upper window.

I opened the full scan. The upper window is empty glass. I took the plate itself to the light box and put the loupe, a small magnifier, on it: a curtain's fold, nothing else. So on Sunday Mr Treloar and I checked every person and sign named in all 480 descriptions against the full scans, about a minute each. 457 names. Twelve of them nobody can find. Then I searched the catalogue.

search "watching from the upper window"   6 plates: 0866 0989 1142 1188 1256 1270
search "standing in the doorway"          3 plates: 0817 1077 1205
search "a board reading ROOMS TO LET"     3 plates: 0852 0934 1103

Six plates, taken years apart, have the same woman at an upper window. Three have a man standing in a doorway that, on the scan, holds a shadow, a coat on a hook, and on plate 1205 a small girl with a basket. Three have a board reading ROOMS TO LET. On plate 0934 the board says SAIL LOFT.
The darkroom keeps developing her, in windows where nobody stood.
Mr Treloar wants the catalogue back online for the heritage open day. What happened, and what do I change?

diagram.aria: Linnet's drawing of plate 1142's trip through the upload script. The full scan, 6384 by 4788 pixels, goes to the script, which shrinks it to 532 by 399, 285 visual tokens, for the model. In that thumbnail the upper window, 150 pixels tall on the scan, is 12.5 pixels tall. The model returns a woman watching from the upper window, and the catalogue records it. Outcomes: under the loupe, a curtain's fold; in the catalogue, 12 of 480 descriptions name someone or something nobody can find.

blocks.caption: Drawn on Sunday from the upload script and the catalogue. Every scan is 6384 by 4788 pixels; the script sends a 532 by 399 thumbnail, 285 visual tokens, at seventeen cents a night for 120 plates. Plate 1142's upper window is 150 pixels tall on the scan and 12.5 in the thumbnail. Of 457 names in the 480 descriptions, 12 are nowhere on the scans: six women at upper windows, three men in doorways, three boards reading ROOMS TO LET.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Glass only holds what the light put there, and a model only sees what your script sends it. A few words for the log. On Anthropic's API a picture goes into the user message as an image content block. The model looks at it in patches of 28 by 28 pixels; each patch is a visual token, billed like any input token. Every model also has a ceiling on how big a picture it takes in: the high-resolution tier, Claude 4.7 and later models, goes to 2576 pixels on the long edge and 4784 visual tokens, the standard tier to 1568 and 1568, and a bigger picture is resized down before the model sees it. Two questions. On the thumbnail your script sent, how many pixels tall is the upper window of plate 1142? And when the model couldn't make out a field, what did your prompt and its fields allow it to write there?

replies.author: u/lightbox_linnet
replies.text: About twelve. The window is 150 pixels tall on the scan, and the thumbnail is a twelfth of the scan's width, so 12.5. As for the fields: the prompt asks for every person and every sign, and each field in the schema is required. A person, a text, or no one. There's nowhere to write can't tell.

comments.author: u/sharper_eyes_kenver
comments.text: Respectfully, this is a model problem, not a pixels problem. A frontier model reads a street sign a cheap one can't, from the very same photo; look at any vision benchmark. Swap the model, keep the thumbnails and the seventeen cents a night. Paying for pictures fifteen times the size, on a tea-room jar, is how volunteer projects die.

comments.author: u/ferry_office_quenby
comments.text: I'm the reader who wrote. My great-grandmother's sister kept the ferry office after the evening boat was lost. The family story is that she watched for it from the upper window every night for years. No photograph of her survives. When the catalogue went online, my mother printed plate 1142 and framed it.

replies.author: u/lightbox_linnet
replies.text: I'm so sorry. I've looked at that window under the loupe three times now. It's a curtain. I'll write to your mother myself.

comments.author: u/ap_desk_ingrith
comments.text: Same thing at work, no ghosts. Our expense app photographs receipts on phones and shrinks them before the model reads them, to save tokens. For a month it returned a delivery charge on receipts that had no delivery, the line that's on most receipts of that kind. Nothing errored. Finance found it when the totals didn't match the card statements.

reply.prompt: Mr Treloar wants the catalogue back online for the heritage open day. What should Linnet change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the thumbnails and move to the strongest model on offer. A better model sees more in the same picture, so the invented people should go, and the bill stays at about seventeen cents a night.
options.part2: I reran the 480 thumbnails on the strongest model the provider offers. The descriptions came back longer and surer: on plate 1142 the woman now wore a dark dress and held the curtain back. Each plate was still 532 by 399 pixels, 285 visual tokens, and the window still 12.5 pixels tall, whichever model read it. In the sim the stand-in has no model setting, because the pixels are the same: 12 invented details, all 12 in the catalogue.
options.senior: A stronger model may guess better, but it can't read pixels that were thrown away before it saw the plate. Anthropic's own limits list says Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes on very small images. Fix what you send first.

options.text: Keep the thumbnails and add a firm line to the prompt: describe only what is really there, and do not hallucinate or invent anyone. The model reads it on every plate, and it costs nothing at all.
options.part2: Same thumbnails, with the line. In the sim the line follows a stated teaching rule: the stand-in leaves a field empty when the detail is at least 14 pixels tall, half of what it needs to read it, and still guesses below that. 7 invented details instead of 12, all 7 in the catalogue, and plate 1142's woman stays: her window is 12.5 pixels tall. The fields still had nowhere to put can't tell.
options.senior: It helps a little. But a line in the prompt can't put a curtain's fold back into 12 pixels, and required fields with no uncertain option demand an answer. Change what the model can see, and what it is allowed to say.

options.text: Stop using the model. Catalogue every plate by hand under the loupe, as the archive did before the script came, so that every person and sign in the catalogue is one that a volunteer has really seen.
options.part2: We tried it for a week: about 20 minutes a plate under the loupe. These 480 plates are 160 hours; the whole archive, 9,600 plates, is 3,200 hours, nearly four years of my four nights a week. Nothing invented, and nothing new in the catalogue for years. The sim shows it for comparison: no tokens, nothing invented, 160 hours.
options.senior: Accurate, and right for the plates that matter most. But it spends a volunteer's years on the 445 details the model read correctly even from a thumbnail. Keep people for checking, not for typing.

options.text: Send each plate at the size the provider's docs recommend, plus crops of any region a description depends on; ask only for what is visible, with can't tell allowed; a volunteer checks each name.
options.part2: Plates now go up at 2128 by 1596, 4332 visual tokens, which the high-resolution tier takes without resizing, image first and then the question. Every field allows can't tell. Any small region the first pass names or can't make out is cropped from the scan at full size and asked again: 7 crops for 480 plates. 0 invented, 449 of 450 real details found, 1 can't tell (plate 1270, a speck 20 pixels tall on the glass), and 449 names checked in 449 minutes. $2.61 a night instead of $0.17. The one it never saw: a dog asleep on the steps of plate 1012, 50 pixels tall, which nothing pointed to.
options.senior: The model can only describe what reaches it. Send pixels the detail survives in, let the model say it can't tell, look closer where a description depends on something small, and have a person confirm every name before it becomes the record.

sim.title: Run the darkroom's last four nights yourself
sim.lede: You're Linnet on Sunday morning with plates 0801 to 1280: 480 plates, four nights of 120, each scanned at 6384 by 4788 pixels. No real model runs here. The stand-in is a script with stated teaching rules: it reads a detail only when the detail is at least 28 pixels tall in the image it was sent, one visual token. Below that, a field that allows can't tell gets can't tell, and a required field gets the most common thing for that kind of region: a woman watching from the upper window, a man standing in the doorway, a board reading ROOMS TO LET. A detail in open street, with nothing to point to it, is simply missed. With do not hallucinate in the prompt, it leaves a field empty when the detail is at least 14 pixels tall. With crops on, every region under 336 pixels on the scan that the first pass named or couldn't make out is cut from the scan at full size, 1064 by 798 (1102 visual tokens), and asked again. The check: a volunteer looks up every person or text named, about a minute each, and strikes what isn't there. Visual tokens follow Anthropic's formula on the high-resolution tier, and the price is the $5 per million input tokens in the example on Anthropic's vision page. 445 people and signs are big enough to read even in a thumbnail.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on the thumbnails, 285 tokens a plate, $0.17 a night: 12 invented details, all 12 in the catalogue, 445 of 450 found. Switch the prompt to do not hallucinate: 7 invented, and plate 1142's woman stays. Allow can't tell instead: none invented, 12 can't tell, still 445 found. Back to required fields, and send the full 2128 by 1596: 4332 tokens, 3 invented (plates 0852, 1256 and 1270), 449 found, $2.60 a night. The whole scan costs more, 4740 tokens, because the provider resizes it to 2212 by 1659, and finds no more. Turn crops on: 7 crops, 1 invented, the speck on plate 1270, $2.61. Allow can't tell: none invented. Turn the check on: 449 names, 449 minutes, 0 errors in the catalogue. Now try the check alone on thumbnails: 0 errors, but 457 minutes and still only 445 found. And half size with crops and can't tell: 448 found for $0.67 a night.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was in the window but a curtain. The script shrank every scan to 532 by 399 pixels, where plate 1142's upper window is 12.5 pixels tall, and the prompt's required fields made the model write something, so it wrote what usually fills an upper window in an old street photograph.

steps.title: A picture goes in as a content block, and it is paid for in patches.
steps.text: On Anthropic's API an image is an image content block in a user message, with one of three source types: a base64-encoded image embedded in the request body, a URL reference to an image hosted online, or a file_id returned by the Files API (upload once, reference many times). Claude supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP. The API takes up to 600 images a request (100 for models with a 200k-token context window), each at most 8000x8000 px and 10 MB base64-encoded. The vision page says Claude views images in patches instead of pixels: each patch is a 28×28-pixel block, a visual token, so an image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens, billed as input tokens. Linnet's thumbnail, 532 by 399, is 19 × 15 = 285; the full send, 2128 by 1596, is 76 × 57 = 4332. Each model has a ceiling: on the high-resolution tier, Claude 4.7 and later models, 2576 px on the long edge and 4784 visual tokens; on the standard tier, all other models, 1568 and 1568. A bigger image is downscaled before the model sees it, keeping its shape, so the whole 6384 by 4788 scan arrives as 2212 by 1659, 4740 tokens: more to upload, nothing more to see. To price it, multiply by the model's price per million input tokens. The page's example is Claude Opus 5 at $5, where a 1000×1000 image costs about $6.48 per thousand. For Linnet's 480 plates that is $0.17 a night for thumbnails and $2.60 for the full send.

steps.title: What the pixels don't hold, the model can only guess.
steps.text: The upper window of plate 1142 is 150 pixels tall on the scan and 12.5 in the thumbnail: less than half of one patch. Whatever the curtain was doing, those pixels can't say. The prompt asked for every person and sign, and the schema made each field required, so the model had to write something, and it wrote what usually fills an upper window in an old street photograph. That is a known failure. Li and colleagues' POPE paper (EMNLP 2023) found that large vision-language models tend to generate objects that are inconsistent with the target images in the descriptions, and that objects that frequently occur in the visual instructions or co-occur with the image objects, are obviously prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs. Anthropic's vision page lists it among Claude's limits: Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes when interpreting low-quality, rotated, or very small images under 200 pixels. OpenAI's guide says the model may generate incorrect descriptions or captions in certain scenarios. This is the hallucination of case 6 of Season 1, with a cause you can measure: the detail was shrunk away before the model saw it. A stronger model reads the same 285 tokens, and a line saying do not hallucinate can't put the curtain back.

steps.title: Ask well: enough pixels, the image first, only what is visible, and a way to say can't tell.
steps.text: Send each plate at a size the tier takes without resizing, and resize it yourself: Anthropic's vision page says to prefer resizing images before uploading them, and its quality guidance says to consider pre-resizing your images, cropping them, or both. Put the image first: Claude works best when images come before text, and if your use case allows it, prefer an image-then-text structure. Ask only for what is visible, and give each catalogue field an uncertain option, an enum value such as can't tell, with the structured output of case 3 of this season, so the model is never forced to fill a field. Where a description depends on something small, look closer. Anthropic's coordinates page says small elements lose precision when an image is downscaled: for fine targets, crop the region of interest and send the crop, or use a high-resolution-tier model. Linnet's script now asks for a rough bounding box around each person or sign it names, and crops any small one from the scan at full size. OpenAI's version is the detail setting on each image: low for coarse image understanding, high, and original for large, dense, spatially sensitive images, which it advises for optical character recognition (OCR) and small-object detection when supported. Its token counts come from 32px x 32px patches on some models, or on others from 512px tiles: 85 base tokens plus 170 a tile for gpt-4o and gpt-4.1. In the sim, the full send with crops and can't tell invents nothing.

steps.title: PDFs and other documents: each page is text and a picture.
steps.text: A PDF goes in as a document content block, with the same three sources: a URL, base64 or a file_id. Anthropic's PDF page says the system converts each page of the document into an image, and the text from each page is extracted and provided alongside each page's image, so Claude can read charts and layouts as well as words. Because it relies on Claude's vision, it has the same limitations as other vision tasks, and it costs both ways: each page typically uses 1,500-3,000 tokens per page depending on content density, plus the image cost of the page. The limits apply to the whole request: 32 MB, and 600 pages (100 when the request's context window is under 1M tokens), and dense PDFs can fill the context window first. Its advice: place PDFs before text in your requests, split large PDFs into chunks when needed, and enable prompt caching for repeated analysis. Plain text files such as .txt, .csv or .md can go in document blocks through the Files API; binary formats such as .xlsx or .docx are not supported in document blocks and must be converted to text or PDF first. As for audio, Anthropic's vision and PDF pages say nothing about it. OpenAI's audio and voice page lists separate routes: file transcription for a transcript of an audio file, audio in Chat Completions for audio input or output in an existing chat app, and voice agents built as speech-to-text, the text-agent workflow, then text-to-speech.

steps.title: A description is a lead, not a fact about the past.
steps.text: Anthropic's vision page ends its limits with: Always carefully review and verify Claude's image interpretations, especially for high-stakes use cases. Do not use Claude for tasks requiring perfect precision or sensitive image analysis without human oversight. A catalogue entry naming a person is that kind of use: families read it as history, and one family framed it. So a volunteer checks every person or text the model names against the full scan before it enters the catalogue, about a minute each, 449 minutes for these 480 plates. Can't tells go on a list for someone with a loupe. An audit sample each month, a few plates checked end to end by someone who didn't do the first check, shows whether the checks are holding. And the catalogue keeps each line's provenance: described from a scan by a model, checked by a volunteer, never presented as what someone saw in 1908.

diagram.aria: The careful catalogue pipeline. Top row: the full scan, 6384 by 4788; your script resizes it to 2128 by 1596, 4332 tokens, which the high-resolution tier takes as it is; the model gets the image first, then the question, with fields that allow can't tell. Bottom row, right to left: crops of small regions, cut from the scan at full size and asked again; the volunteer check of every person or text named; the catalogue, with where each line came from. The pixels decide what can be seen.

notes.text: the pixels decide what can be seen

explain.caption: Read from the top left. The script resizes each scan itself, to a size the high-resolution tier takes without resizing again, and sends the image before the question. The model may answer can't tell. Any small region a description depends on is cut from the scan at full size and asked about again. A volunteer checks every person or text named before the catalogue takes it, and the catalogue records where each line came from.

fix.title: The fix: send pixels the detail survives in, let it say can't tell, look closer, and check every name
fix.text: Resize each scan yourself to a size the model's tier takes without resizing: 2128 by 1596, 4332 visual tokens, on the high-resolution tier. Put the image before the question. Ask only for what is visible, and give every catalogue field an uncertain option, can't tell, in a structured output schema, so no field has to be filled. Have the model return a rough box for each person or sign it names, and crop every small one, and every can't tell, from the scan at full size, then ask again about the crop alone. Before anything enters the catalogue, a volunteer checks every person or text named against the full scan, and can't tells go on a list for the loupe. Audit a sample each month, and record where each line came from. In the sim that is 7 crops, 0 invented, 449 of 450 real details found, 1 can't tell, 449 check minutes and $2.61 a night, against 12 invented details in the catalogue at $0.17.

limits: The stand-in is a script, not a model: its 28-pixel threshold, its guesses and its obedience to can't tell are teaching rules, and real models vary by model, prompt and picture. A model allowed to say can't tell may still guess now and then, which is why the check stays on.

Crops only go where something points. The dog asleep on the steps of plate 1012 is 50 pixels tall on the scan and about 17 in the full send, never noticed and so never cropped: 449 of 450, not 450. Tiling the whole scan into 36 crops of 1064 by 798 would find it, at 39,672 tokens a plate, about nine times the full send. And the check is only as good as the volunteer: it catches named people and text, not a wrong date or a wrong street.

Pixels cost money: the full send with crops is $2.61 a night against $0.17, about fifteen times. In the sim, half size with crops and can't tell finds 448 of 450 for $0.67 a night, a middle road if the jar runs low; it misses the rower on plate 1119 as well as the dog.

explain.seniorTake: A model can only describe the pixels that reach it, and a field that must be filled will be filled. So decide what has to be seen, send it at a size the detail survives, put the image before the question, let the model say can't tell, crop where a description depends on something small, and have a person confirm every name before it becomes the record. A better model and a firmer prompt help after that, not instead of it.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: sending images, and what they cost
realWorld.text: Anthropic's vision page: on the API, provide images to Claude as image content blocks using one of three source types: base64, a URL, or a file_id from the Files API. Claude supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP. Claude views images in patches instead of pixels. Each patch is a 28×28-pixel block of the image, referred to as a visual token, so an image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens. The high-resolution tier, Claude 4.7 and later models, has a 2576 px long edge and 4784 visual tokens; the standard tier, all other models, 1568 px and 1568. Images larger than either limit are downscaled before processing. Its table: a 1000x1000 px image is not resized on either tier and costs 1296 tokens; 3840x2160 becomes 1456x819 px and 1560 tokens on the standard tier, 2576x1449 px and 4784 tokens on the high-resolution tier. Claude works best when images come before text. Its limits include: Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes when interpreting low-quality, rotated, or very small images under 200 pixels.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: how images are resized, and when to crop
realWorld.text: The coordinates and bounding boxes page: Claude finds the largest aspect-preserving size that satisfies both of the model's image limits, the edge limit and the visual token limit, and for nearly all photos and screenshots, the visual token limit is what determines the final size. It gives a reference implementation, and examples: a 1920×1080 screenshot resizes to 1456×819 on the standard tier, and an A4 page scanned at 130 DPI, 1075×1520 pixels, resizes to 924×1307. It notes that small elements lose precision when an image is downscaled: for fine targets, crop the region of interest and send the crop, or use a high-resolution-tier model. An image block can set oversized_image to error, to be rejected rather than silently resized.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: PDFs
realWorld.text: Anthropic's PDF support page: the system converts each page of the document into an image, and the text from each page is extracted and provided alongside each page's image. Each page typically uses 1,500-3,000 tokens per page depending on content density, and because each page is converted into an image, the same image-based cost calculations are applied. Limits: a 32 MB request, and 600 pages per request (100 when the request's context window is under 1M tokens). Its best practices include: place PDFs before text in your requests, split large PDFs into chunks when needed, and enable prompt caching for repeated analysis. Binary formats such as .xlsx or .docx are not supported in document blocks and must be converted to text or PDF first.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: the detail setting and image tokens
realWorld.text: OpenAI's images and vision guide: the detail parameter controls image preprocessing. Supported values depend on the model: low, high, original, or auto, and low does not always use fewer tokens than high. For tasks that require fine visual detail or precise coordinates, such as optical character recognition (OCR), small-object detection, or computer use, use "detail": "original" when supported. Some models tokenize images by covering them with 32px x 32px patches, patch_count = ceil(width/32)×ceil(height/32); other models use a base token count plus tokens for 512px tiles, 85 and 170 for gpt-4o and gpt-4.1. Its limitations: the model may generate incorrect descriptions or captions in certain scenarios, and may give approximate counts for objects in images.

realWorld.title: POPE: models describe objects that aren't there
realWorld.text: Li, Du, Zhou, Wang, Zhao and Wen, Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (EMNLP 2023): LVLMs suffer from the hallucination problem, i.e. they tend to generate objects that are inconsistent with the target images in the descriptions. They found that objects that frequently occur in the visual instructions or co-occur with the image objects, are obviously prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs, and proposed POPE, a polling-based query method, to measure it.

asked: How do you send images or PDFs to a model, and what does it cost?
The model describes things that aren't in the image. What do you change?
interview.answer: An image goes in the user message as a content block, with base64 data, a URL, or a file ID from a files API, and I put it before the question. It's billed as input tokens by size: on Anthropic, one visual token per 28 by 28 pixel patch, so 1000 by 1000 is 1296 tokens, and each model tier has a ceiling, 2576 px and 4784 tokens on the high-resolution tier, above which the provider downscales it. So I resize it myself to the largest size the tier takes, and I don't pay to upload pixels it throws away. OpenAI is similar, with a detail setting and 32-pixel patches or 512-pixel tiles depending on the model. A PDF goes in as a document block: each page becomes an image plus its extracted text, so a page costs its text tokens, typically 1,500 to 3,000, plus the image, within limits of 32 MB and a page count per request. If the model describes things that aren't there, I first check what it actually received: often the detail was resized away, or the image was a thumbnail. Then I fix the request: enough resolution, crops of the regions that matter at full size, ask only for what's visible, and give every structured field an uncertain option, so it isn't forced to fill one. A stronger model or a do not hallucinate line can help, but they don't put pixels back. Finally, anything that will be treated as a fact, a name, an amount, a line item, is checked against something: a person reviews named details, I validate totals, and I audit a sample regularly and label the output as a model's description.

terms.def: Input to a model that isn't only text: images, documents such as PDFs, or audio.
The part of a message that carries a picture on Anthropic's API: type image, with a source that is base64 data, a URL or a file_id.
The part of a message that carries a PDF or text file on Anthropic's API, with a URL, base64 or file_id source.
How a content block carries its file: base64 data inside the request, a URL the provider fetches, or a file_id from the Files API.
A way of writing any file as plain letters, digits and a few symbols so it can travel inside a JSON request. It makes the file about a third bigger.
A web address, such as https://example.com/plate.jpg.
Anthropic's API for uploading a file once and pointing to it in later requests by its file_id, instead of sending the bytes each time.
The ID the Files API returns for an uploaded file, used as a content block's source.
Anthropic's unit for images: one 28 by 28 pixel patch. An image costs ceil(width / 28) x ceil(height / 28) of them, billed as input tokens.
A small square of an image that a model takes in as one unit: 28 by 28 pixels on Anthropic's models, 32 by 32 on some of OpenAI's.
How many pixels an image has, written width by height, such as 2128 by 1596.
A small copy of a picture, here 532 by 399 pixels, a twelfth of the scan's width.
Shrink an image to fewer pixels, keeping its shape. Fine detail can vanish.
Change an image's size in pixels. A provider resizes images that are over a model's limits; you can resize first so you know what it sees.
An image's longer side, in pixels.
Anthropic's image limits for Claude 4.7 and later models: up to 2576 px on the long edge and 4784 visual tokens before downscaling.
Anthropic's image limits for all other models: up to 1568 px on the long edge and 1568 visual tokens before downscaling.
Anthropic model versions. The vision page puts Claude 4.7 and later on the high-resolution tier, and prices Claude Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens.
Here, each scan resized to 2128 by 1596, a third of its width, which the high-resolution tier takes without resizing again.
Cut out one part of an image. A crop of a small region, at full size, shows its detail with far fewer pixels than the whole picture.
One part of a picture that a description depends on, such as a window, a doorway or a sign.
A rectangle a model returns to mark where something is in an image, given as pixel positions.
Here, an allowed answer for a field the model can't make out. It turns a forced guess into an honest blank for a person to look at.
A value in a field's enum, such as can't tell, that lets a model say it doesn't know instead of filling the field.
Putting the image block before the question in a message, which Anthropic says works best.
Resize an image yourself before sending it, so the image you keep is exactly the image the model sees.
A setting on an Anthropic image block. Set to error, an image too big for the model is rejected instead of being quietly downscaled.
Portable Document Format: a file that keeps a document's pages, text and pictures exactly as laid out.
A picture of one PDF page that the provider makes and sends to the model, alongside the page's text.
The text pulled out of a document's pages by software, as opposed to read from a picture of them.
A file stored as raw bytes rather than plain text, such as .xlsx or .docx. Convert it to text or PDF before sending it as a document.
A setting on each image in OpenAI's API, low, high, original or auto, that controls how the image is sized before the model sees it.
On some OpenAI models, a 512 by 512 pixel square of an image, each costing a fixed number of tokens.
Optical character recognition: reading printed or written text from a picture.
OpenAI models that price images as 85 base tokens plus 170 for each 512 pixel tile.
A model's ability to take images as input and describe or answer questions about them.
A language model joined to an image encoder so it can read pictures and write about them.
A vision model naming an object that isn't in the picture.
A polling-based query method from a 2023 paper, built to measure object hallucination in vision-language models.
The image-and-text examples a vision-language model is trained on to follow requests about pictures.
Appear together often, such as a figure and an upper window in old street photographs.
Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, a yearly research conference.
Turning speech in an audio file into written text.
Software that writes down what is said in audio.
An assistant you talk to: speech in, speech out, often built as speech-to-text, a text model, then text-to-speech.
OpenAI's API for chat messages, which can also carry audio input or output.
Here, a person looking up every person or text a model named on the full scan before it enters the catalogue.
A record of where a piece of information came from and who checked it, such as described from a scan by a model, checked by a volunteer.
Cutting a whole image into a grid of crops and sending each, so nothing small is missed. It costs every tile's tokens.
An archive's list of what it holds, with a description of each item.
An early photograph recorded on a sheet of glass, light and dark reversed. Common in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
A flat box with a lamp under frosted glass, for looking at negatives.
A small magnifying glass held close to the eye.
A camera on a stand over a light box, used to scan negatives and documents.
A room without light where photographs are developed, made visible from the exposed plate or film.
Treat an exposed plate or film with chemicals so the picture appears.
A volunteer group that raises money for a local archive.
A day when local archives and old buildings open to the public.
Where tickets for a ferry, a boat that carries people across water on a timetable, were sold.
A long upstairs room where sails are made and mended.
A person who lit gas street lamps each evening.
An app where staff photograph receipts to claim back money they spent for work.
One line on a receipt or invoice: a thing bought, its quantity and its price.
A bill a supplier sends, listing what is owed.
The bank's list of what was paid with a card, used to check claims.
The finance team that pays a company's bills.

atWork: Find a pipeline at work that sends pictures or documents to a model: receipts in an expense app, invoices into accounts payable, scanned forms, screenshots for support. Look at what the model actually receives. Is the image shrunk somewhere, by the app, a phone, or the provider's own resizing, and how many pixels tall is the smallest thing you ask about, the total, a date, a line item, in the image that is sent? Count the visual tokens with the provider's formula and compare a few sizes. Then look at the prompt and the schema: does every field have a way to say can't read or uncertain, or must it be filled? Is the image placed before the question? Where a field depends on a small part of the page, is that part cropped and sent at full size? Then the controls: what checks a line item before it's paid, line items that add up to the printed total, amounts that match the card statement, a person for anything over a limit, and an audit sample each month? And is each extracted value stored as the model's reading of a scan, with the scan kept beside it? Standards-readiness note: if your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes the processing integrity criteria (PI1 in the AICPA Trust Services Criteria), a step that turns images into financial records is in scope, and invented line items are the kind of finding an auditor raises. Build the checks and the audit trail in now, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's expense app photographs receipts on phones and shrinks each photo to 400 pixels wide to keep costs down. Finance has found line items, such as a delivery charge, that aren't on the receipts. Nothing errored. What do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Send enough pixels: a size the small print survives in, up to the model's limit, and crops of the regions that matter at full size
Let it say it can't read something: an uncertain option in each field, and ask only for what is visible
Check the output against what you already know: line items must add up to the printed total and match the card statement
A person reviews what matters, and a regular audit sample shows whether it holds

recall.model: The model is guessing because the detail isn't in the pixels: at 400 pixels wide the small print is a blur, so it writes the line that's usually on receipts like that. First, stop shrinking so hard: send each photo at the largest size the model's tier takes without resizing, and crop the line-item and total area and send it at full size. Second, ask only for what is visible, and give each field an uncertain option, can't read, in the structured output, so it never has to fill one. Third, check the output against what you already know: the line items must add up to the printed total, and the total must match the card statement; anything that doesn't goes to a review queue. Fourth, a person reviews flagged receipts and anything over a set amount, and an audit sample each month shows whether the checks are holding.

recall.prompt: Why does the catalogue say a woman is watching from the upper window of plate 1142?
options: The scan picked up a reflection in the glass plate that looked like a figure at the window
The upload script mixed up plate 1142 with another plate that does show a woman
The model saw a 532-pixel thumbnail where the window was 12.5 pixels tall, and required fields made it guess
The negative really holds a faint figure that only the model's training could pick out
recall.why: The window is 150 pixels tall on the scan and 12.5 in the thumbnail, less than half of one 28-pixel patch, so the detail wasn't there to read. The prompt's fields were required, with no way to say can't tell, so the model wrote what usually fills an upper window in old street photographs. Under the loupe the plate shows a curtain's fold, and at the full send the window reads as empty.

recall.prompt: A teammate asks how you send a picture or a PDF to a model, and what it costs. Walk them through it.

keyIdeas.idea: It goes in the message as a content block, carrying base64 data, a URL or a file_id
Images are billed as input tokens by size: on Anthropic, one visual token per 28 by 28 pixel patch
Images over the model's limits are downscaled, so resize first and don't pay for pixels it throws away
A PDF page is sent as extracted text plus an image of the page, so each page costs both

recall.model: A picture goes in the user message as an image content block, carrying base64 data, a URL, or a file_id from the Files API, and it works best placed before the question. It's billed as input tokens by its size: on Anthropic's models each 28 by 28 pixel patch is one visual token, so the cost is ceil(width / 28) times ceil(height / 28). Each model tier has limits, a long edge and a visual token count, and anything bigger is downscaled before the model sees it, so resize it yourself and don't pay to upload pixels it throws away. A PDF goes in as a document block: the provider turns each page into a page image and sends the extracted text alongside, so each page costs its text tokens, typically 1,500 to 3,000, plus the image cost.

recall.prompt: Using Anthropic's formula, how many visual tokens does a 1000 by 1000 pixel image cost on either tier?
options: 1000, one for each row of pixels
recall.why: Each visual token is a 28 by 28 patch: ceil(1000 / 28) is 36, and 36 times 36 is 1296, the figure in Anthropic's own table. It isn't resized on either tier, since 1296 is under both 1568 and 4784 and the long edge is under 1568 px. At Claude Opus 5's $5 per million input tokens that is about $6.48 per thousand images.

recall.prompt: What does Anthropic's API give the model for each page of a PDF you send?
options: An image of the page, with the page's extracted text alongside it
Only the text it can extract, so charts and photos are lost
A summary of the page written by a smaller model first
The raw bytes of the PDF file, which the model reads directly
recall.why: Anthropic's PDF page: the system converts each page of the document into an image, and the text from each page is extracted and provided alongside each page's image. That's why Claude can answer about charts, and why each page costs text tokens, typically 1,500-3,000, plus the image cost.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The catalogue has been back online since the open day, every name checked, and the checks have found nothing invented since spring. Now the Friends have been given the old ferry company's ledgers: 2,400 handwritten pages from 1890 to 1914, scanned into PDFs. Mr Treloar wants the model to transcribe every passenger's name and fare from them, and to stop the volunteer checks, since they never find anything any more.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell Mr Treloar, and how would you set up the ledgers?

keyIdeas.idea: Price and size the PDFs first: every page is a page image plus extracted text, so count the tokens, and split the ledgers under the page and request limits
Handwriting needs pixels and honesty: render pages at a size the writing survives, crop the columns, and let every field say can't read
Don't stop the checks: they find nothing because they are there; keep a sample audit and check the names that matter
Never present a transcription as fact: record it as the model's reading of a scan, with its source and who checked it

coldCase.model: Price it before promising it. Each PDF page goes to the model as a page image plus extracted text, and handwriting gives little usable extracted text, so count the tokens on a few pages, then work out the cost per page and split the 2,400 pages into chunks under the page and request limits. Handwriting needs pixels: render the pages yourself at a size the writing survives, crop the name and fare columns at full size, put the image before the question, and give every field a can't read option, so a faded name becomes a blank for a volunteer rather than a guess. Don't stop the checks: they find nothing because they are there, and a ledger of names is exactly where a guess becomes someone's family history. Keep checking every name that goes public, and keep a sample audit of a few pages a month. And never present a transcription as fact: mark each entry as a machine transcription from a named source scan, checked by a named volunteer.

sources.title: Anthropic, Vision (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: image content blocks with base64, URL or file_id sources; Claude works best when images come before text; up to 600 images per API request (100 for models with a 200k-token context window), 8000x8000 px and 10 MB base64-encoded per image on the API; JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP; Claude views images in patches, each a 28×28-pixel block referred to as a visual token, so an image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens; high-resolution tier (Claude 4.7 and later models) 2576 px long edge and 4784 visual tokens, standard tier (all other models) 1568 px and 1568; larger images are downscaled; 1000x1000 px costs 1296 tokens; Claude Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens on the high-resolution tier, about $6.48 per thousand 1000×1000 images; prefer resizing images before uploading them; Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes when interpreting low-quality, rotated, or very small images under 200 pixels; always carefully review and verify Claude's image interpretations, especially for high-stakes use cases

Anthropic, Coordinates and bounding boxes (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: how Claude resizes and pads images, the largest aspect-preserving size within the edge limit and the visual token limit, with a reference implementation; 1920×1080 resizes to 1456×819 and 1075×1520 to 924×1307 on the standard tier; small elements lose precision when an image is downscaled: for fine targets, crop the region of interest and send the crop, or use a high-resolution-tier model; oversized_image set to error rejects instead of resizing

Anthropic, PDF support (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: PDFs as document content blocks by URL, base64 or file_id; maximum request size 32 MB; 600 pages per request (100 when the request's context window is under 1M tokens); the system converts each page into an image and the text from each page is extracted and provided alongside each page's image; subject to the same limitations as other vision tasks; each page typically uses 1,500-3,000 tokens per page depending on content density, plus image-based costs; place PDFs before text, split large PDFs into chunks, enable prompt caching for repeated analysis; .xlsx and .docx are not supported in document blocks and must be converted to text or PDF first

OpenAI, Images and vision (API docs), read 11 October 2026: images by URL, Base64-encoded data URL or file ID; the detail parameter controls image preprocessing, with low, high, original or auto depending on the model, and low does not always use fewer tokens than high; use detail original for OCR, small-object detection or computer use when supported; 32px x 32px patches, patch_count = ceil(width/32)×ceil(height/32), on some models; base tokens plus 512px tiles on others, 85 and 170 for gpt-4o and gpt-4.1; limitations include incorrect descriptions or captions in certain scenarios and approximate counts

OpenAI, Audio and voice (API docs), read 11 October 2026: for transcription, translation, or speech generation without a conversational agent, choose the dedicated API; file transcription for a transcript of an audio file; audio in Chat Completions for audio input or output in an existing chat app; voice agents as speech-to-text, the text-agent workflow, then text-to-speech

Li, Du, Zhou, Wang, Zhao and Wen, Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models, EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.10355): LVLMs tend to generate objects that are inconsistent with the target images in the descriptions; objects that frequently occur in the visual instructions or co-occur with the image objects, are obviously prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs; POPE, a polling-based query method
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including the additional criteria for processing integrity, PI1
